description: Labelled turns for testing the LinguaTrace note-taker. Each case states what a competent tutor would expect the notebook to record. Negative cases matter as much as positive ones: a note-taker that fires on every line is noise.

turn.speaker: learner
turn.text: Yesterday I go to the office.

context.speaker: learner
context.text: Yesterday I go to the office.

turn.speaker: tutor
turn.text: Yesterday I went to the office. With 'yesterday' the verb moves to the past.

turn.speaker: learner
turn.text: My manager asked me to present the numbers to the team.

turn.speaker: tutor
turn.text: Hi Ana, good to see you again.

context.speaker: learner
context.text: Sometimes I cannot find the word and I stop.

turn.speaker: tutor
turn.text: There is a useful expression for that: 'to draw a blank'. It means your mind goes empty.

turn.speaker: tutor
turn.text: That sounds like a difficult week. What happened on Tuesday?

turn.speaker: learner
turn.text: I want to speak confidently in meetings before my review in June.

turn.speaker: tutor
turn.text: We should keep working on past tenses before the next lesson.

context.speaker: learner
context.text: I had three presentations last month.

turn.speaker: tutor
turn.text: Perfect, that is exactly right. Well done.

turn.speaker: learner
turn.text: He go to work every day by train.

context.speaker: learner
context.text: He go to work every day by train.

turn.speaker: tutor
turn.text: He goes to work every day by train.

cases.note: A single error type, so the label is unambiguous.

turn.speaker: tutor
turn.text: And what did you say to your manager?

cases.note: Two error types in one sentence. Either label is defensible, so this case checks only that a correction is detected at all.

context.speaker: learner
context.text: Last month I has three presentations and all of them was stressful.

turn.speaker: tutor
turn.text: Last month I had three presentations and all of them were stressful.

cases.note: Observed on a live call: the learner talking about the app was written up as a language mistake.

turn.speaker: learner
turn.text: What is the difference between 'since' and 'for'?

cases.note: Observed: with no preceding turn this scored 0.36 and the learner's practice was discarded.

turn.speaker: learner
turn.text: What you also see here is that um use cases I would categorize them in tiers. I would have use cases that can be fully automated, for example like the tracking status

cases.note: Observed end to end: 'go becomes went' became a flashcard glossed as 'se convierte en'.

context.speaker: learner
context.text: Yesterday I go to the office.

turn.speaker: tutor
turn.text: Yesterday I went to the office. When you use yesterday, the verb moves into the past, so go becomes went.

turn.speaker: tutor
turn.text: It went well. We use well for how something happened, and good for describing a thing.

cases.note: Observed end to end: 'it will come with practice' was logged as something to practise.

turn.speaker: tutor
turn.text: It is the most common thing learners slip on, and it will come with practice.
